title: Pain Scales: Yeeeow!
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss pain scales and how doctors measure pain. They cover why pain is subjective and hard to quantify, the American Pain Society's description of pain as the fifth vital sign, and US pain prevalence statistics. The history includes the 1940 dolorimeter built by James Hardy, Harold Wolf and Helen Goodell at Cornell, Dr. Lauren Bella Glutzek's chin-pressure device, and Dr. Kenneth Keel's proposal to simply ask patients to rate pain on a numeric scale. They describe self-reported scales (numeric, word-based, and the worst pain imaginable), the Wong-Baker FACES scale developed with Donna Wong and Connie Baker for children, and observational tools based on behavioral and physiological cues. Examples include the nonverbal CNPI checklist for cognitively impaired elderly and the CRIES tool for infant pain. The episode also covers patients under-reporting or over-reporting pain, fentanyl-laced heroin, needle phobia, and a listener email about psychology and pacifism.
topics: pain in dementia and cognitive impairment

segments.title: Opening banter and pain topic setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, including Josh joking about hitting his hand with a hammer, and introduce the episode on pain scales as a way of quantifying pain.

segments.title: Why pain is hard to measure and prevalence
segments.summary: The hosts explain that no physical instrument accurately measures pain, so doctors rely on self-report and observation. They note that pain is subjective, that the medical community has historically undertreated pain, and that the American Pain Society calls pain the fifth vital sign. They cite US statistics on acute and chronic pain.

segments.title: Early pain measurement: the dolorimeter
segments.summary: In 1940, researchers James Hardy, Harold Wolf and Helen Goodell at Cornell built the dolorimeter, a heat lamp used on volunteers (described as nurses or doctors' wives, some pregnant) to compare heat to labor pain, with a unit called the dol. The device could not be reproduced by other doctors. Dr. Lauren Bella Glutzek later built a chin-pressure device reported in Time Magazine, and Kenneth Keel proposed simply asking patients to rate pain on a numeric scale.

segments.title: Self-reported pain scales and med-seeking concerns
segments.summary: Chuck explains that Keel's self-reported scale caught on in the 1960s, usually as a 0-to-10 or 0-to-100 scale. The hosts discuss patients who exaggerate pain to get drugs, the importance of honest reporting, and the opioid problem with fentanyl-laced heroin.

segments.title: Word scales, children and the Wong-Baker FACES chart
segments.summary: Word-based scales run from no pain to intolerable, and the worst pain imaginable is discussed. The hosts note that injuries like burns may hurt most. They describe the Wong-Baker FACES scale, developed in the early 1980s by Donna Wong and Connie Baker, which children helped refine, and explain why tears were kept on the chart.

segments.title: Observational pain assessment and special populations
segments.summary: When self-report is unreliable because of age, language, culture, or cognitive impairment, doctors observe behavioral and physiological cues such as grimacing, guarding, sweating, and changes in heart rate. The CNPI checklist for cognitively impaired elderly patients is described, along with the CRIES tool for infants, which scores crying, oxygen saturation, vital signs, expression and sleeplessness.

segments.title: Needle phobia and personal anecdotes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss childhood needle fear, under-reporting pain to avoid shots, modern thin needles and blood draw tubes, and Josh's anecdote about working on pediatric hospital projects and observing adults and children in pain.

segments.title: Listener mail from Scott Miller
segments.summary: A listener praises the show, mentions his background as a behavior analyst pursuing a PhD, and shares his views on pacifism.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to social media and the website for more information.
